impacts.caseName: Teva Pharmaceuticals International GmbH v. Eli Lilly and Company
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court erred in granting judgment as a matter of law that Teva's headache patents claiming methods of treating headache using humanized anti-CGRP antagonist antibodies were invalid for failure to satisfy the written-description and enablement requirements of 35 U.S.C. § 112.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the district court's JMOL of invalidity for Teva's headache patents, which cover methods of using humanized anti-CGRP antagonist antibodies to treat headache. A jury had found willful infringement and no invalidity, but the district court overturned that verdict on written-description and enablement grounds. This decision reinstates patent protection for a significant class of biologic drug patents.
impacts.positiveImplications: Strengthens patent protection for biopharmaceutical companies holding genus claims on antibody-based therapeutics, particularly where the specification discloses known methods of making and humanizing antibodies, even if only one specific antibody is exemplified.
impacts.negativeImplications: Generic and biosimilar drug developers face continued barriers to market entry where broad antibody method-of-treatment claims survive validity challenges under § 112.

impacts.caseName: VLSI Technology LLC v. Intel Corporation
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court correctly granted summary judgment of noninfringement of the '836 patent based on extraterritoriality and rejection of VLSI's doctrine of equivalents theory, and whether the court properly struck certain damages expert theories.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed in part the district court's summary judgment of noninfringement of VLSI's multicore processor patent asserted against Intel, finding error in at least one of the noninfringement grounds. The court also addressed the propriety of striking damages expert theories for inadequate disclosure in damages contentions. The case involves high-stakes semiconductor patent litigation between a major patent assertion entity and a leading chipmaker.
impacts.positiveImplications: Provides clarity on the application of extraterritoriality doctrine in patent infringement cases involving semiconductor design and manufacturing, potentially expanding the scope of domestic patent enforcement for technology companies.
impacts.negativeImplications: Technology companies with global manufacturing and design operations face increased exposure to patent infringement claims where components or processes touch the United States, even if significant activity occurs abroad.

impacts.caseName: Versata Software, LLC v. Ford Motor Company
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court erred in excluding Versata's trade secret damages expert testimony and in overturning the jury's breach of contract damages award, and whether Ford was entitled to JMOL on trade secret misappropriation liability.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the district court's judgment on trade secret damages and remanded for a new trial, instructing the court to reconsider two previously rejected damages models. The court reversed the district court's judgment on breach of contract damages and reinstated the jury award. The court affirmed liability for trade secret misappropriation under both the DTSA and Michigan UTSA. This case involved Ford's development of replacement software after licensing Versata's automotive configuration software.
impacts.positiveImplications: Software licensors and trade secret owners benefit from the court's recognition that multiple damages methodologies may be appropriate in trade secret cases and that jury verdicts on contract damages should not be lightly overturned.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies that license third-party software and subsequently develop in-house replacements face significant trade secret misappropriation risk, with potentially broader damages exposure under reinstated damages models.

impacts.caseName: International Medical Devices, Inc. v. Cornell
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether there was a legally sufficient evidentiary basis for the jury's finding that the asserted trade secrets were protectable under California law, and whether the patent-invalidity claims based on inventorship were properly decided.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the denial of JMOL on trade secret misappropriation claims, holding that the plaintiffs failed to show the asserted trade secrets were protectable because the information was generally known. The court also reversed on patent invalidity, finding the alleged inventor's contribution consisted of generally known ideas insufficient for inventorship. The counterfeiting claim and damages were affirmed. The permanent injunction and exemplary damages on trade secrets were vacated.
impacts.positiveImplications: Defendants in trade secret cases benefit from heightened scrutiny of whether asserted information truly qualifies as a protectable trade secret versus generally known information in the field.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies relying on trade secret protection for product designs and manufacturing processes must ensure robust evidence that their claimed secrets are not generally known in the industry, or risk losing both trade secret and related patent claims.

impacts.caseName: Insulet Corp. v. EOFlow, Co. Ltd.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the statute of limitations under the Defend Trade Secrets Act had expired before Insulet brought suit alleging that EOFlow misappropriated trade secrets related to its insulin patch pump technology.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the district court's denial of JMOL, holding that the three-year DTSA statute of limitations had expired before Insulet filed suit. Despite jury findings of misappropriation and that the claim was timely, the court concluded as a matter of law that Insulet knew or should have known of the misappropriation more than three years before filing. This eliminates a substantial damages judgment and permanent injunction against EOFlow.
impacts.positiveImplications: Companies accused of trade secret misappropriation benefit from strict enforcement of the DTSA's three-year statute of limitations, particularly where the trade secret owner had early indicators of potential misappropriation but delayed filing suit.
impacts.negativeImplications: Trade secret owners must act promptly upon discovering or having reason to discover misappropriation; delay in filing DTSA claims risks complete loss of remedy even where misappropriation is proven on the merits.

impacts.caseName: Constellation Designs, LLC v. LG Electronics Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patents claiming non-uniform constellations for digital communication systems are patent-eligible under 35 U.S.C. § 101, and whether the district court properly denied JMOL on infringement and damages.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the summary judgment of patent eligibility for certain claims of the '761 and '700 patents relating to non-uniform constellations in digital communications, while affirming eligibility for claims of the '509 and '922 patents. The court affirmed the denial of JMOL on non-infringement and damages. This case has significant implications for patent eligibility of innovations in wireless communications standards used in consumer electronics.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders in communications technology standards benefit from the affirmance of eligibility for certain patent claims and the affirmance of a willful infringement finding and damages award against a major electronics manufacturer.
impacts.negativeImplications: Consumer electronics manufacturers implementing industry standards face continued patent infringement exposure, with the court requiring further proceedings on eligibility for some claims rather than invalidating them outright.

impacts.caseName: Ollnova Technologies Ltd. v. Ecobee Technologies ULC
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the jury verdict on patent infringement must be vacated where the verdict form asked a single question covering infringement for all asserted patents without identifying which patents were infringed, and whether the § 101 analysis for the '495 patent was properly conducted.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the $11.5 million infringement and damages judgments and remanded for a new trial, finding that the verdict form's single infringement question covering all four asserted patents was fatally flawed. The court also vacated and remanded for further proceedings on the § 101 analysis for the '495 patent, while affirming that the '887 and '371 patents survived the abstract idea inquiry under Alice step one. This case involves patents on wireless building automation systems asserted against smart thermostat products.
impacts.positiveImplications: Accused infringers benefit from the requirement that jury verdict forms must separately identify infringement findings for each asserted patent, preventing ambiguous aggregate verdicts.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders asserting multiple patents risk losing favorable jury verdicts if verdict forms do not separately track infringement findings per patent, requiring more careful trial management and potentially multiple trials.

impacts.caseName: AGI SureTrack LLC v. Farmers Edge Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patents claiming automated systems for capturing, processing, and sharing farming data using relay devices attached to farming equipment are directed to patent-ineligible subject matter under 35 U.S.C. § 101, and whether the case is exceptional under 35 U.S.C. § 285.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed that AGI's asserted farming data collection patent claims are patent-ineligible under § 101, finding them directed to the abstract idea of collecting, processing, and sharing farming data. The court vacated the district court's determination that the case was not exceptional and remanded for reconsideration of attorney fees under § 285. This decision reinforces limits on patenting data collection and processing methods in agricultural technology.
impacts.positiveImplications: Technology companies defending against patents claiming conventional data collection methods applied to specific industries benefit from continued strict application of Alice/Mayo eligibility analysis, with potential recovery of attorney fees.
impacts.negativeImplications: Agtech companies and other businesses seeking to patent data collection and processing systems face heightened § 101 eligibility risks, and patent holders asserting such claims face potential exceptional case findings and fee awards.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a Rule 30(b)(6) corporate representative may testify at summary judgment outside of personal knowledge to establish pre-critical-date sales for purposes of the on-sale bar under 35 U.S.C. § 102(b), and whether source code constitutes hearsay.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed summary judgment of invalidity under the on-sale bar, holding that a 30(b)(6) corporate representative may testify about historical company sales even without personal knowledge. The court also held that computer source code commands are not hearsay statements. These evidentiary rulings facilitated invalidation of patents on engine controller reprogramming technology based on prior commercial sales.
impacts.positiveImplications: Accused infringers benefit from the expanded ability to use 30(b)(6) deposition testimony and source code evidence to prove prior art defenses, particularly the on-sale bar, even when original engineers are unavailable.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders face broader evidentiary challenges to validity at summary judgment, as corporate designees may testify about historical product sales without personal knowledge and source code is admissible as non-hearsay.

impacts.caseName: A.L.M. Holding Company v. Zydex Industries Private Ltd.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a patent owner that grants an exclusive license but retains the right to sue for infringement and other exclusionary rights has sufficient constitutional standing to bring a patent infringement suit.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the district court's dismissal for lack of standing, holding that patent owners who retain the right to sue third parties for infringement possess a sufficient exclusionary right to satisfy Article III standing requirements, even when they have granted an exclusive license to a third party. This clarifies standing doctrine for patent owners with complex licensing arrangements.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent owners with exclusive licensing agreements who retain enforcement rights can proceed with infringement actions without joining the licensee, providing flexibility in monetizing and enforcing patent portfolios.
impacts.negativeImplications: Accused infringers lose a procedural defense based on standing challenges in cases where the patent owner retains enforcement rights under a licensing agreement.

impacts.caseName: Ascendis Pharma A/S v. BioMarin Pharmaceutical Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a respondent in an ITC proceeding may obtain a mandatory stay under 28 U.S.C. § 1659(a)(2) of a refiled declaratory judgment action involving the same parties, after having missed the deadline for seeking a stay of its original declaratory judgment action.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit held that an ITC respondent cannot circumvent the mandatory stay deadline under § 1659(a)(2) by voluntarily dismissing and refiling a declaratory judgment action. BioMarin filed an ITC complaint against Ascendis, which then filed a declaratory judgment action but missed the 30-day stay deadline. BioMarin's attempt to dismiss and refile to obtain a mandatory stay was rejected. This ruling prevents gamesmanship in coordinating parallel ITC and district court proceedings.
impacts.positiveImplications: Declaratory judgment plaintiffs (often accused infringers or generic drug applicants) are protected from strategic manipulation of mandatory stay provisions, ensuring their district court actions proceed without improper delay.
impacts.negativeImplications: ITC complainants and patent holders cannot use the refiling of district court actions to reset mandatory stay deadlines, limiting their ability to delay parallel district court proceedings while ITC investigations are pending.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the ITC correctly found that Apple's importation and sale of Apple Watch models with blood oxygen measurement features violated Section 337 of the Tariff Act by infringing Masimo's patents on wearable blood oxygen measurement devices.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the ITC's finding that Apple violated Section 337 and upheld the limited exclusion order barring importation of infringing Apple Watch models with blood oxygenation features. The court found no error in the Commission's domestic industry determination, validity rulings, or infringement findings regarding Masimo's patents covering wearable pulse oximetry technology. This is one of the highest-profile ITC exclusion orders affecting a major consumer electronics product.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders and domestic manufacturers benefit from strong enforcement of ITC exclusion orders against major importers, reinforcing the ITC as an effective forum for protecting U.S. intellectual property rights.
impacts.negativeImplications: Major technology companies face significant product exclusion risk at the ITC when incorporating patented health-monitoring features into consumer devices, potentially requiring design-arounds or licensing arrangements to maintain market access.

impacts.caseName: Federal Express Corporation v. Qualcomm Incorporated
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a non-party to underlying patent litigation may file an IPR petition on the same patents on behalf of the litigant to circumvent the one-year time bar under 35 U.S.C. § 315(b), and whether the Board's obviousness determination was supported by substantial evidence.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the Board's obviousness determination and remanded, finding issues with the Board's analysis of the challenged claims of FedEx's sensor-based logistics patent. Qualcomm filed IPR petitions on the last day of Roambee's filing deadline, despite not being a party to the underlying litigation. The court addressed both the propriety of such filings and the substantive obviousness analysis, with significant implications for IPR practice and proxy petitioning.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent owners benefit from closer scrutiny of proxy IPR petitions filed by non-parties that appear designed to circumvent the statutory time bar, potentially limiting abusive IPR filings.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies that rely on third-party IPR petitions as a defensive strategy face increased uncertainty about the permissibility of such filings when they appear to be coordinated with time-barred parties.

impacts.caseName: Fortress Iron, LP v. Digger Specialties, Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a district court may correct patent inventorship under 35 U.S.C. § 256(b) when a known co-inventor cannot be located, and whether patents are invalid for omitting an unreachable co-inventor.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the invalidation of two patents for failure to name a co-inventor who could not be located after leaving his employer. The court also affirmed the denial of the patent owner's motion to correct inventorship under § 256(b), as the patent owner could not satisfy the statutory requirements without the missing inventor's participation. This case highlights the critical importance of properly identifying and maintaining contact with all inventors.
impacts.positiveImplications: Accused infringers can challenge patent validity based on omitted inventors, even where the omission was not deceptive, providing a powerful defense when inventorship is incomplete.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies collaborating with foreign manufacturers and contractors face patent invalidation risk if co-inventors from partner organizations cannot be located to correct inventorship, underscoring the need for robust inventor identification and contact-maintenance practices.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court properly approved a $125 million class action settlement of claims that the federal judiciary unlawfully used PACER fees to fund expenses unrelated to the PACER system, and whether incentive awards to class representatives were permissible.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the district court's approval of a $125 million nationwide class action settlement resolving claims that the federal judiciary overcharged PACER users by using fees to fund unrelated judicial technology expenses. The court upheld the settlement terms, attorneys' fee awards, and incentive awards to the three nonprofit class representatives. Hundreds of thousands of PACER users will receive full or substantial reimbursement for fees paid during the eight-year class period.
impacts.positiveImplications: The settlement provides a model for resolving government overcharge class actions and confirms that incentive awards to nonprofit class representatives are permissible, encouraging public-interest organizations to serve as class representatives.
